_note: Module 16 of docs/PROMPT-CONTROL-TOWER-UI.md (§7.3, §8): the query-to-voice mapping the GilbertOne API Administration Voice screen would read. Proposed 24 September 2026, Phase 2 of that plan — a contract and its build checks, and nothing else. No screen reads this file, no route serves it, and apps/assistant-api/src/lib/voice-config.ts, the service the plan names for it, does not exist. What this file adds is the thing the plan asks for before any screen: which kinds of answer may have their voice configured, by whom, and which may not be configured at all. It holds no voice. Every voice name, every locale a voice exists for, the cloud voice's own pair, the push-to-talk and caption decisions and the 30-second and 45-second caps already live in packages/catalog/assistant.json#voice, decided by the founder on dated records there, and this file points at them rather than typing them again — scripts/check-boundaries.mjs fails the build if a neural voice name appears here. How GilbertOne speaks today, as read from the tree on 24 September 2026: one voice for everything a platform says. The web asks the browser for a voice in voice.voicePreference's order; the phones use their own on-device synthesiser in the same order; where the cloud voice is configured — it is, in production, in southafricanorth only (docs/governance/ASSISTANT-ACTIVATION.md) — POST /assistant/v1/speak reads with one of the two en-ZA voices in voice.cloud.voices, or an Afrikaans voice for an Afrikaans answer. No kind of answer has a voice of its own. So the lock below is not a lock on something that varies today; it is the rule that no configuration may ever give an emergency, a refusal or an escalation a voice chosen for presentation.
_statusWhy: The plan's own vocabulary (docs/PROMPT-CONTROL-TOWER-UI.md §2): declared in a contract, not built. The voice itself — browser, phone and cloud — is built and answers patients; what is proposed is the per-class mapping, the per-tenant provider choice and the preview panel. There is no tenant, so there is no per-tenant anything yet (packages/catalog/gilbertone-inference-isolation.json).
_gateWhy: docs/PROMPT-CONTROL-TOWER-UI.md §9: the clinical-delivery register reviewed by layer 4 (Clinical Administrator) through the Clinician Review Queue; §07's V03 refusal unchanged; the push-to-talk constraint in a contract. This file puts the third in a contract and scripts/check-boundaries.mjs holds the second. The first has not happened: the queue has never received an entry, and the governance board that would ratify one is recorded as not formed in packages/catalog/protocols.json#governance.

reads.why: Every fact the Speech settings screen needs that already has a home is read from it. A second copy of a voice name is a second answer to 'which voice reads an emergency in South Africa', and the day the two disagree nobody can say which was the decision.

zones.label: Clinical delivery
zones.sentence: Emergency, refusal and escalation answers are read in a neutral, clear register. Their voice is not configurable by a tenant, an administrator or a user. Rate and pitch may be adjusted for accessibility; nothing else about how they sound may be.
zones.why: An emergency answer read in a warm presentation voice at a comfortable pace is an emergency answer that sounds less urgent than it is. How the words that send somebody to an ambulance sound is part of what they say, so changing it is a clinical change and moves through the one door clinical changes move through.

zones.label: Clinical assist
zones.sentence: Answers that assist a clinician are available only when a clinician is signed in. Nobody is signed in to anything today: packages/catalog/intelligence-levels.json records that no clinician session exists for the lock to read.
zones.why: A register written for a nurse reading a result is not a register for a patient reading about themselves, and the only thing that can tell the two audiences apart is a signed-in clinician, which does not exist yet.

zones.label: Presentation
zones.sentence: Routine answers, navigation, what a signed-out visitor hears and what an administrator hears may have their voice set from the two voices packages/catalog/assistant.json lists for each language that has one. No tenant exists, so the platform default is the administrator's setting on the Control Tower — one of the four presentation-voice settings in this file's settings block, changed on the Speech settings screen and on the Configuration tab — and it is the language's female voice until an administrator changes it, as the founder decided on 27 September 2026.
zones.why: How the booking steps or a greeting sound is a brand decision a hospital may reasonably want to make, and it changes nothing a clinician would have to review.

queryClasses.label: Emergency
queryClasses.why: The answer with the ambulance numbers in it. It is decided at level 0 by the deterministic layer and read in the locked register; the preview panel plays it so an administrator hears the boundary, and offers no Save as default on this row.

queryClasses.label: Refusal
queryClasses.why: A refusal that sounds apologetic or playful reads as negotiable. The words are the contract's; the register keeps them sounding like what they are.

queryClasses.label: Escalation
queryClasses.why: Telling somebody to be seen today is a clinical act the Tier 1 ruleset decides. Its sound is locked for the same reason its words are.

queryClasses.label: Clinical assist
queryClasses.why: Its level is decided by who is signed in, which intelligence-levels.json owns; this file only says its voice is not a tenant's to set.

queryClasses.label: Routine
queryClasses.why: Everyday answers from the catalogue: what a visit costs, what to expect.

queryClasses.label: Navigation
queryClasses.why: Where a screen is and how to get there.

queryClasses.label: Signed-out visitor
queryClasses.why: What somebody on the public page hears before they have an account. Its voice may be presented; its level may not rise above 1, which packages/catalog/intelligence-levels.json holds and scripts/check-boundaries.mjs cross-checks from here.

queryClasses.label: Admin
queryClasses.why: What an administrator hears in the Control Tower. Nothing here is a patient's.

clinicalDeliveryRegister.sentence: Neutral, clear and unambiguous: the words at the pace the listener set, without warmth added or urgency removed.
clinicalDeliveryRegister._pinnedHashWhy: The first 16 hex characters of the SHA-256 of this register's sentence and the three clinical-delivery classes above, serialised as scripts/check-boundaries.mjs serialises them. The build recomputes it: any edit to those classes or this sentence fails until the pin is changed with it, and a pin other than version 1's founding value is refused unless ratifiedEntryRef names the Clinician Review Queue entry that allowed it — the same way packages/catalog/gilbert-clinical-core.json pins escalation.ts. The queue has no runtime store yet, so the build can require the reference but cannot look it up; that is said here rather than implied.
clinicalDeliveryRegister._reviewedByWhy: Nobody clinical has reviewed this register. Locked is not the same as reviewed — packages/catalog/gilbert-clinical-core.json's locked-is-not-the-same-as-clinically-reviewed refusal, restated for sound.

providers._perTenantWhy: The plan asks for a provider chosen per tenant. There is no tenant, so there is one choice per direction, made by configuration on the box: api-registry.json's speechSelection names the two variables (MYTHUSO_STT_PROVIDER, MYTHUSO_TTS_PROVIDER) and the default, azure-speech, which answers when both its variables are set and its region is southafricanorth. Each id above is a card in api-registry.json, which says of each whether it is built and whether it is configured: since 28 September 2026 azure-speech, openai-whisper, alibaba-qwen-asr, alibaba-qwen-tts and elevenlabs are built, and only azure-speech is configured. Since the same day the text-to-speech provider for each presentation register is an administrator's setting below (presentation-provider-routine and the other three), applied by the service only where the residency decision admits the provider; the clinical-delivery registers always read through the default. A built provider with no South African region is refused in production for these routes while the residency decision is blank; the registry's own refusal says so.
providers.onDeviceConversationMode: The founder's speech amendment of 21 September 2026 (CLAUDE.md) keeps cloud voices out of the on-device conversation mode — ElevenLabs is named there — and keeps Azure Speech's two routes as the server-side fallback. A cloud TTS or STT card in the registry is never a route for the on-device mode, whatever its status.

tts.who: tenant for presentation classes; user for every class
tts.why: Speed is an accessibility axis before it is a style: somebody with a processing difficulty needs slower speech on an emergency answer most of all.

tts.who: tenant for presentation classes; user for every class
tts.why: Some hearing losses lose one end of the range; pitch is how a listener brings the words back into it.
Volume is the phone's or the browser's, and no setting here may make an emergency answer quieter than the device is set to.

stt.why: The locales the service already accepts; a hint outside them is a language nothing downstream can answer.
Not decided. The browser and the phones decide when a capture ends today; a server-side threshold arrives with a server-side stream, which does not exist.

Not decided. The panel shows what was heard for correction before anything is sent (voice.correctionBeforeSend); interim results would change what is on the screen while somebody is still speaking, which is a design decision, not a default.

keysAndRegions.sentence: A provider's key and the region it is called in are lines in the service's environment on the box, entered by hand through deploy/ops/configure-assistant-env.sh. No setting holds either, no screen shows either, and the region a patient's voice goes to is a residency decision the responsible party and the Information Officer sign, not a knob.
keysAndRegions.why: A key in a setting is a key in a history table that every admin reads. A region in a setting is a cross-border transfer made by whoever holds the screen.

speakingStyle.sentence: Azure Speech's expressive styles — cheerful, calm, and the rest — are not a setting: neither of the two South African English voices nor either Afrikaans voice on file lists one, so there is nothing to choose, and the clinical-delivery register would refuse it if there were.
speakingStyle.why: A style setting with one allowed value is a control that can never change, and a control that can never change is drawn as a sentence.

utteranceCap.sentence: The 45-second cap on one push-to-talk capture is the founder's speech amendment of 21 September 2026 (CLAUDE.md), read from packages/catalog/assistant.json#voice, and no setting moves it.
utteranceCap.why: A founder decision, not an edit.

speechToTextProvider.sentence: Which provider hears a patient's capture is written by hand on the box (MYTHUSO_STT_PROVIDER, packages/catalog/api-registry.json#speechSelection) and is not a setting: a capture is a patient's voice, which is health information, and where it goes is decided by the people the residency decision names.
speechToTextProvider.why: The registry's own reason: selecting where a patient's voice goes is a decision written by hand, like the production acknowledgement.

pushToTalk.sentence: Tap to speak, and tap Stop to finish. The microphone opens only because somebody tapped it, and closes on its own after the cap in packages/catalog/assistant.json#voice. There is no setting that removes the tap.
pushToTalk.why: The plan (§7.3) asks for push-to-talk as a locked setting, not a toggle. Every microphone any platform opens today is opened by a tap; the build holds that the gesture recorded in assistant.json still includes push-to-talk, and that no application wires a wake word.

captions.sentence: The written words stay on the screen in full, before the voice starts and for as long as it speaks. Nothing turns them off.
captions.why: A spoken reply is a second reading of the words, never a replacement for them — the founder's rule of 20 September 2026. A person who cannot hear, or who is somewhere the voice cannot be heard, reads exactly what everybody else hears.

wakeWordQuestion.sentence: No application listens for a wake word. packages/catalog/assistant.json records voice.wakeWord as true and the gesture as wake-word-with-push-to-talk-fallback, from the founder's speech amendment of 21 September 2026, and packages/gilbertone/src/speech-state.ts carries a state machine with wake-word events — but no web, iOS or Android file wires one, so what patients reach is push-to-talk only.
wakeWordQuestion.discrepancy: docs/PROMPT-CONTROL-TOWER-UI.md §7.3 says 'no wake word, no passive recording, no background listening' and calls this the 22 September founder direction. No record of a 22 September direction on the wake word was found in the tree on 24 September 2026; the only dated record is the 21 September amendment, which says the opposite. This file does not choose between them. Until the founder records which stands, scripts/check-boundaries.mjs fails the build if any application wires wake-word detection.
wakeWordQuestion.why: An always-available microphone changes the privacy posture in front of the Information Regulator even when nothing leaves the device (CLAUDE.md's DPIA caution). A question that large is not settled by whichever document a builder read last.

questions: What does this voice sound like?
How does it sound on my own sentence, including one in a South African language?
How does it sound on the answers that matter — the same sentence in the emergency, refusal and routine registers?
How does it compare with two or three alternatives on the same sentence?
What does it cost, and how fast is it?

rejectsPatientIdentifiers.sentence: This preview does not read text that looks like a person's details. Remove the name, number or identity number and try again.
rejectsPatientIdentifiers.why: An administrator testing a voice on a real case note is the most natural mistake in the world. The same redactor the assistant service runs on every turn decides what looks like an identifier, so the preview and the service cannot disagree about it.

costAndLatency.why: No price has been measured through this panel and no latency has been measured at all. The estimate the panel shows before Play — since 27 September 2026 — is a list price copied by hand onto the provider's card in packages/catalog/api-registry.json (pricing), multiplied by the sentence's characters; it is what a reading would cost at the published rate, never what one did. A measured figure arrives with a bill that has been read, and this value stays null until one has.

languages.sentence: A language with ttsAvailable false has no voice anywhere in MyThuso, and the Speech settings screen marks it not available rather than hiding it. Its answers are shown as text, with voice.voiceUnavailableNotice.
languages.why: §07's V03 refusal stands: no voice is chosen by locale setting and no South African voice is promised to be installed. isiZulu, isiXhosa and Sesotho are understood and not spoken, and the screen says so in the contract's own words.

refusals.statement: An emergency, refusal or escalation answer is never read through a provider, at a speed, a pitch, a style or in a voice that a setting chose. It is read by the platform default provider in the language's own voice at the voice's own pace.
refusals.why: How an emergency answer sounds is part of what it says. Every provider and tuning setting names the presentation registers alone, the guardrails forbid the clinical classes, and the service applies tuning only where the request names a presentation register.

refusals.statement: No setting holds a provider's key or the region it is called in, and no screen draws either.
refusals.why: A key in the settings history is a key every administrator reads; a region in a setting is a border crossed by whoever holds the screen. Both are environment lines on the box, and where a voice goes is a residency decision.

refusals.statement: A provider with no South African region may be chosen for a register on this screen and, in production, is refused by the service until the residency decision is signed: the platform default reads the answer instead, and the refusal is printed at start-up.
refusals.why: The setting is the administrator's to make and the transfer is the responsible party's to approve. The screen records the first; the service enforces the second in the registry's own sentence, and no setting overrides it.

refusals.statement: When a spending ceiling is reached the cloud voice stops and the answer stays written on the screen. Nothing is ever withheld from a person because a budget ran out.
refusals.why: The written words are the answer; the voice is a second reading of them. A ceiling on the second reading is a ceiling on money, not on care.

refusals.statement: The own-voice feature is switched on and off by an administrator only, reads only the presentation registers, and never carries a voice that is not the administrator's own.
refusals.why: The founder's decision of 28 September 2026. A patient is never offered a person's voice; a clinical answer is never read in one; and recording somebody else's voice needs consent this setting cannot hold.

refusals.statement: A speak request that names no register is read by the platform default provider with no tuning, and one that names a register the contract does not have is refused.
refusals.why: Tuning follows the register, and a request that will not say which register it is for is not trusted to be a presentation one.

refusals.statement: An emergency, refusal or escalation answer is never read in a voice a tenant, an administrator or a user chose. Rate and pitch may change; the voice may not.
refusals.why: How an emergency answer sounds is part of what it says. A setting that could make it sound calmer than it is would be a clinical change made in a brand menu.

refusals.statement: The clinical-delivery register changes only through a ratified entry in the Clinician Review Queue, recorded by raising its version and naming the entry.
refusals.why: The same door escalation.ts and the emergency terms move through (packages/catalog/clinical-review-queue.json no-auto-promotion-without-a-signature). A second, quieter door for how those words sound would be a way round the first.

refusals.statement: The preview plays the emergency, refusal and escalation registers so they can be heard. It never offers to save a voice as their default.
refusals.why: Hearing the boundary is the point of the preview; a Save button on that row would present a locked setting as a configurable one.

refusals.statement: Push-to-talk is shown as a locked setting, never a toggle. No screen offers to keep the microphone open.
refusals.why: A toggle is an invitation to switch it. The microphone opens because somebody tapped it, and that is not something a tenant configures on a patient's behalf.

refusals.statement: The written words are never switched off. There is no caption toggle, for a tenant or a user.
refusals.why: A spoken reply is another reading of the words, not a replacement for them.

refusals.statement: This file names no voice. Voices are read from packages/catalog/assistant.json, per language, and nowhere else.
refusals.why: The plan's wireframes name voices the catalogue does not hold. Which voice reads a health answer in South Africa is a decision already on file in one place.

refusals.statement: The preview refuses text that looks like a person's details, using the service's own redactor.
refusals.why: An administrator's test sentence becomes audio at a provider. A patient's details have no business being that sentence.

refusals.statement: No preview plays through a paid provider without showing its estimated cost first, and the panel keeps a running total for the session.
refusals.why: A preview button that spends money without saying so is a bill somebody discovers later.

refusals.statement: No application listens for a wake word while the founder's two records on it disagree.
refusals.why: An always-listening microphone is a change of privacy posture that needs one decision on file, not two that contradict each other.

refusals.statement: A presentation voice setting reaches routine answers, navigation, what a signed-out visitor hears and what an administrator hears. It never reaches an emergency, refusal or escalation answer, whatever it is set to.
refusals.why: The four settings below each name one presentation class and nothing else, and the clinical-delivery classes are pinned by hash with no setting at all. A change on the Configuration tab moves how a greeting sounds; it cannot move how the words that send somebody to an ambulance sound.

_speakTextMaxWhy: The most one call to POST /v1/speak may ask to be read, added on 1 October 2026. A spoken answer is words that already exist: the longest the catalogue writes is under seven hundred characters and a model's reply is capped at twelve hundred, so five thousand carries any answer whole. Above it the service refuses with the route's own payload-too-large before any provider is asked or the month's ceiling is spent, so one request cannot read a novel aloud on the founder's account.

ownVoice.sentence: An administrator may have a provider read the presentation registers in the administrator's own recorded voice. Only an administrator changes it, and today the only administrator is the founder.
ownVoice.whoseVoice: The administrator who switches it on, recording their own voice in the provider's own console with their own consent; today the founder.

consent.recordedBy: The setting's own history: the change that switched it on names the administrator, the day and the reason, and stands as the consent of the person whose voice it is, because it is the same person.
consent.anotherPerson: Refused. A voice that is not the administrator's own — a nurse's, an actor's, a patient's — is not switched on here: recording it needs that person's written consent and a decision about who owns the voice, neither of which this setting can hold.

ownVoice.howItIsNamed: The provider's identifier for the recorded voice is a line in the service's environment on the box (the card's environment in packages/catalog/api-registry.json), never a value in this repository or on a screen: it identifies a person's voice, and the on-device conversation mode and the phones' own synthesisers never see it.
ownVoice.neverFor: An emergency, a refusal or an escalation: the clinical-delivery register is pinned by hash above and no provider setting reaches it. A patient is never offered a person's voice as a choice.
ownVoice.why: The founder's instruction of 28 September 2026: the own-voice features are only the admins who can change that, meaning currently the founder. Written here so the build can hold it — the setting's changedBy is admin, the guardrail forbids every clinical class, and the identifier is read by the adapter alone.

settings._note: The founder decided on 27 September 2026 that the four presentation registers above — routine, navigation, signed-out visitor and admin — are an admin setting, under the standing rule that an open policy question becomes an admin setting with a proposed default: which of the two voice labels every language with a voice carries in packages/catalog/assistant.json#voice.languages[].ttsVoices reads that register, with the language's female voice as the default. A value is a label and never a voice name; whoever speaks resolves it per language, and a language with ttsAvailable false stays text whatever the label says. The clinical-delivery classes and clinical assist are not here and cannot be added here: their register is pinned by hash above. In this preview a change is kept in this tab's memory for the session, and the shipped default is this contract's.
settings.heading: GilbertOne voice and speech settings
settings.intro: Which of a language's two voices reads each presentation register, which provider reads it and how — speed, pitch, encoding, ElevenLabs' own knobs — the ceilings on what the cloud voice may spend, and the administrator's own voice. Emergency, refusal and escalation answers are not here, because how they sound is not a setting.

allowed.proposedBecause: Built 28 September 2026 on the founder's ask. No South African region: in production the service refuses it while the residency decision is blank and the register falls back to the platform default, saying so at start-up.

allowed.label: Alibaba Qwen-TTS
allowed.proposedBecause: Built 28 September 2026. Singapore or Beijing and nowhere in South Africa, so the same production refusal applies; it speaks English of the contract's languages and no other.

items.appliesTo: The next spoken answer of that register. In production a provider with no South African region is refused by the service while docs/governance/DATA-RESIDENCY-OPTIONS.md §7 is blank, and the answer is read by the platform's default provider instead — the refusal is printed at start-up and nothing is sent offshore. An emergency, refusal or escalation answer never asks this setting: it is read by the platform's default provider whatever is chosen here.

guardrail.statement: An emergency, refusal or escalation answer is never read through a provider a setting chose, and a provider that is not built is never chosen.

items.label: Fall back to the platform default provider
items.help: When the provider chosen for a register is not configured, is refused in production or does not answer, does the platform default read the answer instead?

default.proposedBecause: A spoken answer that falls silent because a second provider was misconfigured is the browser's own voice reading the same words, which is the fault the cloud voice exists to end. Falling back to the platform default keeps the reading, and the start-up line says which provider was refused.

allowed.label: Yes, the platform default reads it
allowed.proposedBecause: The reading is kept.

allowed.label: No, the answer stays written
allowed.proposedBecause: For a deployment that would rather show the words than pay a second provider for them.

items.appliesTo: The next spoken answer of a presentation register whose provider did not answer. The clinical registers always read through the platform default and never ask this.

items.label: Spoken answers a month
items.help: How many characters may the cloud voice read in a calendar month before spoken answers stop and answers stay written?

default.proposedBecause: Two million characters is about thirty-two US dollars at Azure's recorded list price and about two hundred at ElevenLabs' pay-as-you-go rate: enough for a month of a small service, and small enough that a runaway loop cannot spend a quarter's budget in a night. A ceiling in characters rather than money, because that is what every provider bills and no currency has to be converted.

lowest.proposedBecause: Ten thousand characters is a day of use; below it the ceiling would silence the voice on the first morning.

highest.proposedBecause: A hundred million characters is more than any provider's largest plan includes; above it the ceiling would not be one.

items.appliesTo: Counted by the service per calendar month, across every provider, with a reading's characters held against the ceiling while the provider is asked so that readings arriving together cannot pass it between them. The month's count is kept in the service's state directory, so a restart carries on from it; a service started without one counts from the moment it started, and says so rather than pretending to remember. When the ceiling is reached the speak route refuses in its own sentence and the answer stays written; the browser's own voice may still read it. The words are never withheld: only the paid reading stops.

guardrail.statement: The ceiling stops sound and never words: an answer is always written on the screen whatever the count.

items.label: Preview per administrator session
items.help: How many characters may the Speech settings screen's preview read in one session before Play is refused?

default.proposedBecause: Twenty thousand characters is about a hundred sentences: a long afternoon of comparing voices, and a fraction of a dollar at either provider's rate.

lowest.proposedBecause: A few sentences; below it the preview could not compare two voices on one paragraph.

highest.proposedBecause: A million characters in one session is a preview being used as a reading service.

items.appliesTo: The preview panel's Play, counted in the tab's memory for the session. Reaching it disables Play with the panel's own sentence; nothing already playing stops. It never touches a patient's reading, only the administrator's preview.

items.label: Azure speaking speed
items.help: How fast does Azure Speech read a presentation register, as a percentage of the voice's normal speed?

default.proposedBecause: The voice's own pace until somebody has listened at the edges. Sent to Azure as an SSML prosody rate only when it is not a hundred, so the default changes nothing about what is sent today.

lowest.proposedBecause: Thirty percent slower is the slowest a sentence stays a sentence; below it the words come apart. A proposal until the founder has listened.

highest.proposedBecause: Thirty percent faster is the fastest a second-language listener can follow a health answer. A proposal until the founder has listened.

items.appliesTo: The next Azure reading of a presentation register. The clinical-delivery registers are read at the voice's normal pace whatever this says; a person's own accessibility speed is packages/catalog/user-preferences.json's axis, not this setting.

guardrail.statement: An emergency, refusal or escalation answer is never read faster or slower by a tenant's setting.

items.label: Azure pitch
items.help: How high does Azure Speech read a presentation register, as a percentage of the voice's normal pitch?

default.proposedBecause: The voice's own pitch. Sent as an SSML prosody pitch only when it is not a hundred.

lowest.proposedBecause: Twenty percent lower keeps a neural voice sounding like itself; a proposal until listened to.

highest.proposedBecause: Twenty percent higher, for the same reason.

items.appliesTo: The next Azure reading of a presentation register, and never a clinical-delivery one.

guardrail.statement: An emergency, refusal or escalation answer is never pitched by a tenant's setting.

items.label: Azure audio quality
items.help: What does Azure Speech encode a reading as — lighter on a metered phone, or fuller on a good connection?

default.proposedBecause: The format packages/catalog/assistant.json#voice.cloud.outputFormat decided on 22 September 2026, restated here as the default and held equal to it by the build: about 360 kilobytes a minute.

allowed.label: Lighter — 16 kHz, 32 kbit/s, about 240 kB a minute
allowed.proposedBecause: For a patient on a mid-range phone on metered data, who this is built for.

allowed.label: Standard — 24 kHz, 48 kbit/s, about 360 kB a minute
allowed.proposedBecause: The decided default.

allowed.label: Fuller — 24 kHz, 96 kbit/s, about 720 kB a minute
allowed.proposedBecause: For an administrator's preview on a desk, comparing voices.

items.appliesTo: The next Azure reading of any register: an encoding changes how much data a phone downloads, not how the words sound, so the clinical registers follow it too. It never changes which voice reads or how it sounds.

items.label: Azure recognition of strong language
items.help: When somebody swears into the microphone, does Azure hand back the word, mask it or drop it?

default.proposedBecause: The person corrects the transcript on the screen before anything is sent, so masking edits their words before they have seen them; and a swear word about a symptom is part of the symptom.

allowed.label: Hand back the word as heard
allowed.proposedBecause: What the person said.

allowed.label: Mask it with asterisks
allowed.proposedBecause: For a deployment whose transcripts are read aloud in a shared room.

allowed.label: Drop it
allowed.proposedBecause: For a deployment that would rather lose the word than show it.

items.appliesTo: The next capture Azure hears. Sent as the recognition request's profanity parameter. Every capture, whatever register the conversation is in; it never edits the words after the person has seen them.

items.label: Time allowed to voice one stretch
items.help: How long may a provider take to read one stretch of an answer before the service gives up and the browser's own voice carries on?

default.proposedBecause: The ceiling apps/assistant-api/src/lib/providers/seam.ts has carried since 22 September 2026, restated here and held equal by the build: one call is one stretch of a sentence, and a caller wanting sound sooner asks for the next stretch itself.

lowest.proposedBecause: Below five seconds a provider on a slow evening never answers.

highest.proposedBecause: A minute is longer than any reading; above it a hung provider holds the panel silent.

items.appliesTo: Every speak call started after the change, whichever provider reads. Never a call already under way.

items.label: Time allowed to hear one capture
items.help: How long may a provider take to turn one push-to-talk capture into words before the service gives up?

default.proposedBecause: The ceiling seam.ts has carried since 22 September 2026, held equal by the build: a full capture is uploaded and read in one request.

lowest.proposedBecause: A forty-five-second capture cannot be read in under ten.

highest.proposedBecause: Above a minute a hung recogniser holds the panel with nothing to show.

items.appliesTo: Every listen call started after the change, whichever provider hears. Never a call already under way.

items.label: ElevenLabs model
items.help: Which ElevenLabs model reads an answer?

default.proposedBecause: The vendor's own default for the text-to-speech route on the day recorded, and the model whose overage price the card records. Flash halves the cost and the latency at some quality; v3 adds Afrikaans and is charged at the same rate as v2.

allowed.label: Multilingual v2 — 29 languages, English of the contract's
allowed.proposedBecause: The vendor's default.

allowed.label: Flash v2.5 — 32 languages, English of the contract's, lowest latency, half the price
allowed.proposedBecause: For a deployment that wants the reading to start sooner.

allowed.label: Eleven v3 — 70 and more languages, English and Afrikaans of the contract's
allowed.proposedBecause: The one model the vendor lists Afrikaans for, read from the vendor's own list on 28 September 2026.

items.appliesTo: The next ElevenLabs reading. A language the chosen model does not list is answered as having no voice, and the words stay on the screen. The words always stay on the screen.

items.label: ElevenLabs stability
items.help: How steady is the ElevenLabs voice between readings — high for the same delivery every time, low for more expression?

default.proposedBecause: The vendor's documented default. A health answer read the same way every time is what a listener can rely on.

lowest.proposedBecause: The vendor's range is nought to one, sent here as a percentage.

highest.proposedBecause: The vendor's range is nought to one, sent here as a percentage.

items.appliesTo: The next ElevenLabs reading of a presentation register, sent in the request's voice settings. A clinical-delivery register is read at the vendor's own defaults whatever this says.

items.label: ElevenLabs similarity
items.help: How closely does ElevenLabs hold to the chosen voice's own sound?

default.proposedBecause: The vendor's documented default.

lowest.proposedBecause: The vendor's range is nought to one, sent here as a percentage.

highest.proposedBecause: The vendor's range is nought to one, sent here as a percentage.

items.appliesTo: The next ElevenLabs reading of a presentation register, sent in the request's voice settings. A clinical-delivery register is read at the vendor's own defaults whatever this says.

items.label: ElevenLabs style exaggeration
items.help: How much does ElevenLabs amplify the voice's own style — nought for none?

default.proposedBecause: The vendor's documented default, and the only value under which a presentation voice stays plain. The clinical registers never read through this setting at any value.

lowest.proposedBecause: The vendor's range is nought to one, sent here as a percentage.

highest.proposedBecause: The vendor's range is nought to one, sent here as a percentage.

items.appliesTo: The next ElevenLabs reading of a presentation register, sent in the request's voice settings. A clinical-delivery register is read at the vendor's own defaults whatever this says.

items.label: ElevenLabs speaker boost
items.help: Does ElevenLabs boost the similarity to the chosen speaker, at a cost in latency?

default.proposedBecause: The vendor documents the boost as adding latency, and a reading that starts sooner matters more to somebody waiting for a health answer than a closer likeness.

allowed.label: On
allowed.proposedBecause: A closer likeness to the chosen voice.

allowed.label: Off
allowed.proposedBecause: A reading that starts sooner.

items.appliesTo: The next ElevenLabs reading of a presentation register. It never reaches an emergency, refusal or escalation answer.

items.label: ElevenLabs speaking speed
items.help: How fast does ElevenLabs read a presentation register, as a percentage of the voice's normal speed?

default.proposedBecause: The voice's own pace, sent as the vendor's speed multiplier of one.

lowest.proposedBecause: The vendor's documented range for a voice's speed setting is 0.7 to 1.2, read on 28 September 2026.

highest.proposedBecause: The vendor's documented range for a voice's speed setting is 0.7 to 1.2, read on 28 September 2026.

items.appliesTo: The next ElevenLabs reading of a presentation register, and never a clinical-delivery one.

guardrail.statement: An emergency, refusal or escalation answer is never read faster or slower by a tenant's setting.

items.label: ElevenLabs audio quality
items.help: What does ElevenLabs encode a reading as — lighter on a metered phone, or fuller on a good connection?

default.proposedBecause: The lightest MP3 the vendor documents, about 240 kilobytes a minute, because the patient this is built for is on a mid-range phone on metered data. The vendor's own default is the fullest.

allowed.label: Lighter — 22 kHz, 32 kbit/s, about 240 kB a minute
allowed.proposedBecause: For a metered phone.

allowed.label: Standard — 44 kHz, 64 kbit/s, about 480 kB a minute
allowed.proposedBecause: A middle setting.

allowed.label: Fuller — 44 kHz, 128 kbit/s, about 960 kB a minute
allowed.proposedBecause: The vendor's default, for a desk comparing voices.

items.appliesTo: The next ElevenLabs reading of any register: an encoding changes how much data a phone downloads, not how the words sound. It never changes which voice reads or how it sounds.

items.label: ElevenLabs latency mode
items.help: How much of the vendor's latency optimisation is asked for — nought for none, four for the most, at which its text normaliser is switched off?

default.proposedBecause: No optimisation: the vendor documents that the highest level switches its text normaliser off, and a health answer with a dose in it needs its numbers read as numbers.

lowest.proposedBecause: The vendor's documented range, read on 28 September 2026.

highest.proposedBecause: The vendor's documented range, read on 28 September 2026.

items.appliesTo: The next ElevenLabs reading, sent as the request's optimize_streaming_latency parameter. Every register, because it changes when the reading starts and never how it sounds.

guardrail.statement: A level the vendor does not document is never sent.

items.label: The administrator's own voice
items.help: Which presentation registers does the administrator's own recorded voice read, where a provider carries it?

default.why: The founder's decision of 28 September 2026: the own-voice feature is an administrator's setting and nobody else's, and today the only administrator is the founder. It starts off, because no recorded voice exists in any provider account until the founder records one there, with the consent packages/catalog/voice.json#ownVoice records.

allowed.label: Off — the language's own voices read every register
allowed.proposedBecause: Nothing here names a person's voice.

allowed.label: The administrator's own register only
allowed.proposedBecause: What an administrator hears in the Control Tower, and nothing a patient hears.

allowed.label: Every presentation register
allowed.proposedBecause: Routine answers, navigation, the signed-out visitor and the administrator. Never an emergency, a refusal or an escalation.

items.appliesTo: The next spoken answer of the registers chosen, only where that register's provider is one that carries a recorded voice (ElevenLabs today) and the service's environment names the voice; otherwise the language's own voice reads it and nothing fails. The clinical-delivery registers never ask this setting.

guardrail.statement: An emergency, refusal or escalation answer is never read in a person's own voice, and no clinical register is offered here.

changelog.why: The founder's decision of 27 September 2026 that the four presentation registers are an admin setting, each starting on the language's female voice. The clinical-delivery registers are not in this log and never will be: they are not settings.

The founder approved the speech-settings scope of 28 September 2026: ElevenLabs built beside Azure Speech and Alibaba Qwen-TTS, every knob either provider exposes that is not a key, a region or a clinical register made an administrator's setting with a proposed default, and the own-voice feature an administrator's alone. Every default below is a proposal until the founder has listened at the edges, except own-voice, which the founder decided.

preview: The Speech settings screen exists — the Voice screen was folded into it on the founder's instruction of 28 September 2026 — and each of the four presentation registers has a setting an administrator changes on it and on the Configuration tab, kept in this tab's memory for the session or, inside the founder's signed-in session, in the assistant service's own history. The clinical-delivery registers have no setting, no tenant has chosen anything, and no preview has been played through a paid provider. Since 28 September 2026 the Speech settings screen and the Configuration tab carry the provider per presentation register, Azure's and ElevenLabs' tuning, two ceilings and the administrator's own voice, kept the same way; ElevenLabs is built and configured nowhere, and the service reads every one of these settings from the contract's defaults until it holds a settings history of its own. The voices GilbertOne speaks in today are the browser's, the phone's and, in production, the cloud pair in packages/catalog/assistant.json.
